mainTopic: Openings to the מגילה and a word-by-word reading of its first פסוק
overview: This amud first lists many 'openings' (פתיחתות) to the מגילה. In each one, a חכם takes a verse from elsewhere in תנ״ך and shows that it hints to the פורים story: fire, water and abundance; a roaring lion and a hungry bear; laziness in Torah; 'a man and not a king'; and the joy of שושן. Then the גמרא starts explaining the first פסוק of the מגילה word by word. רב reads ויהי as a cry of woe, and שמואל and a ברייתא bring a verse showing that God never abandons ישראל in exile, sending מרדכי and אסתר in the days of המן. Four חכמים find hidden meanings in the name אחשורוש, and the word 'הוא' teaches that wicked people stayed wicked and righteous people stayed righteous, with דוד staying humble even as king. The גמרא then discusses 'המולך', 'מהודו ועד כוש' (with a parallel argument about שלמה), and the 127 provinces, which רב חסדא says came in three stages. The amud ends with a ברייתא naming three kings who ruled the whole world: אחאב, אחשורוש and נבוכדנצר.

steps.title: A verse from עזרא points to the time of המן
steps.stepSummary: This amud opens with the end of an earlier opening: the verse in עזרא about God's kindness to us before the kings of פרס, which the גמרא says refers to the days of המן.
steps.simpleTranslation: "For we are slaves, yet in our slavery our God did not abandon us, and He gave us kindness before the kings of פרס." When did this happen? In the time of המן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes an opening that was started on the previous amud. It quotes a verse from עזרא and says it is talking about the days of המן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says God was kind to us 'before the kings of פרס' while we were still slaves in exile. The גמרא asks which moment this fits, and answers: the פורים story, when a king of פרס saved the Jews instead of destroying them.

keyTerms.meaning: When? The גמרא's way of asking which historical moment a verse is about
Slavery or servitude, here meaning life in exile
The kings of Persia, such as אחשורוש

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The kindness 'before the kings of פרס' in עזרא refers to the salvation in the days of המן.

steps.title: Fire, water, and abundance: three periods of danger and rescue
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר פפא opens the מגילה with a verse in תהלים. 'Fire' is נבוכדנצר, 'water' is פרעה, and 'You brought us out to abundance' is the days of המן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר פפא opened this section with this verse: "You let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and water." 'Through fire' means in the days of wicked נבוכדנצר. 'Through water' means in the days of פרעה. 'And You brought us out to abundance' means in the days of המן.
steps.whatsHappening: A new חכם gives his own opening to the מגילה. He reads a verse in תהלים as a map of three moments in Jewish history, and the last of them is פורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each piece of the verse is matched to an enemy. נבוכדנצר threw חנניה, מישאל and עזריה into a fiery furnace, and פרעה threw the baby boys into the river. The happy ending, 'abundance', is the פורים rescue, a story full of feasts.

keyTerms.meaning: He opened with an introduction, meaning he began his teaching with an outside verse
The section, here meaning מגילת אסתר
From here, meaning from the following verse
Abundance or fullness, literally being satisfied with drink

steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the verse in תהלים, fire is נבוכדנצר, water is פרעה, and the abundance is the rescue in the days of המן.

steps.title: The whole world saw God's salvation in the days of מרדכי and אסתר
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן opens with a verse in תהלים that says all the ends of the earth saw God's salvation, and says this happened in the days of מרדכי ואסתר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן opened this section with this verse: "He remembered His kindness and faithfulness to the house of ישראל; all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God." When did all the ends of the earth see the salvation of our God? In the days of מרדכי and אסתר.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opening. רבי יוחנן asks when the whole world saw a Jewish salvation, and answers that it was in the פורים story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most salvations were local events, but the verse says the whole earth saw it. In the פורים story, the king's letters went out to all 127 provinces, so the danger and the rescue really were known everywhere.

keyTerms.meaning: His faithfulness, meaning God keeps His promises
The ends of the earth, meaning the whole world

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan opened with an introduction

phrases.english: all the ends of the earth saw

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another opening from a different verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The salvation that 'all the ends of the earth saw' is the salvation in the days of מרדכי ואסתר.

steps.title: ריש לקיש's verse: the roaring lion is נבוכדנצר
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש opens with a verse in משלי about a roaring lion, a hungry bear, and a wicked ruler. He first identifies the lion as נבוכדנצר, using a verse in ירמיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש opened this section with this verse: "A roaring lion and a hungry bear: a wicked ruler over a poor nation." 'A roaring lion' is wicked נבוכדנצר, as it is written about him: "A lion has come up from his thicket."
steps.whatsHappening: A fourth opening begins. ריש לקיש quotes his verse and starts explaining it piece by piece, beginning with the lion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To show that the lion means נבוכדנצר, he brings a second verse (ירמיה) where the prophet calls נבוכדנצר a lion. The bear is explained in step 5, and the wicked ruler and the poor nation in step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: A poor, weak nation, meaning the Jewish people
As it is written about him, which introduces a supporting verse

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another opening from a different verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'roaring lion' in משלי is נבוכדנצר, as ירמיה calls him a lion.

steps.title: The hungry bear is אחשורוש
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש continues: the 'hungry bear' is אחשורוש, because in דניאל the second kingdom, Persia, is pictured as a bear.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A hungry bear' is אחשורוש, as it is written about him: "And behold, another beast, a second one, resembling a bear."
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש moves to the next part of his verse and identifies the bear as אחשורוש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In דניאל's vision of four beasts, the second beast is a bear and stands for the kingdom of פרס. אחשורוש was the king of פרס, so the bear in משלי is him.

phrases.english: "A hungry bear" is Achashverosh,
as it is written about him:
"And behold, another beast, a second one,
phrases.notes: This is in דניאל, chapter 7: a vision of four beasts that stand for four kingdoms.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'hungry bear' is אחשורוש, based on דניאל's image of פרס as a bear.

steps.title: רב יוסף: why the Persians are compared to a bear
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that the bear in דניאל means the פרסיים, and he lists four ways they are like bears: eating and drinking, heavy flesh, long hair, and never resting.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יוסף taught: These are the Persians, who eat and drink like a bear, are covered with flesh like a bear, grow their hair long like a bear, and have no rest like a bear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching of רב יוסף to back up the idea that the bear in דניאל stands for the פרסיים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the bear image is not random: the Persians really act like bears in four ways. It supports ריש לקיש's claim that the bear is אחשורוש, the Persian king. Step 7 then finishes ריש לקיש's opening by explaining the 'wicked ruler' and the 'poor nation'.

keyTerms.meaning: Taught, used when a teaching from the time of the תנאים is quoted
Covered with flesh, meaning heavy and fat

phrases.english: And Rav Yosef taught:
These are the Persians,
who eat and drink like a bear,
and are covered with flesh like a bear,
and grow hair like a bear,
and have no rest like a bear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up step 5 by showing that the bear in דניאל really means the פרסיים.
steps.raayaObject: That the 'bear' in דניאל, and so in ריש לקיש's verse, refers to פרס and its king אחשורוש.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יוסף's teaching listing four bear-like traits of the פרסיים.
steps.whatToRemember: Each opening takes an outside verse and shows that it hints to the פורים story: עזרא (kindness before the kings of פרס), רבי חנינא בר פפא (fire, water, abundance), רבי יוחנן (the whole world saw), and ריש לקיש (lion = נבוכדנצר, bear = אחשורוש; step 7 adds wicked ruler = המן).

steps.title: The wicked ruler is Haman and the poor people is Israel
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש finishes explaining the verse in משלי: the 'wicked ruler' is המן, and the 'poor people' is ישראל, who were poor in מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A wicked ruler' means המן. 'Over a poor people' means ישראל, because they were poor in keeping the מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes ריש לקיש's line-by-line reading of the verse. After the lion and the bear, he now explains the last two parts of the verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lion was נבוכדנצר and the bear was אחשורוש. Now the 'wicked ruler' is המן. The 'poor people' are not poor in money. They are poor in מצוות, which hints at why they were open to danger.

keyTerms.meaning: poor in מִצְוֹת, meaning weak in keeping them

steps.confusionAlert: 'Poor' here is not about money. It means ישראל was lacking in מצוות.

phrases.english: "A wicked ruler" — this is Haman.
"Over a poor people" — these are Israel,
phrases.notes: This is still the same verse in משלי about the lion and the bear.

phrases.english: who are poor in מצוות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes ריש לקיש's explanation of the משלי verse after the side point by רב יוסף about the bear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the verse, the wicked ruler is המן and the poor people is ישראל, who were lacking in מצוות.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר's opening: laziness in Torah weakened Israel's protection
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר opens the מגילה with a verse in קהלת about laziness making the roof sink. He explains that because ישראל was lazy in Torah, it was as if הקדוש ברוך הוא became 'poor' and could not help them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר opened this section with the verse: 'Through laziness the rafters sink, and through idle hands the house leaks.' Because ישראל was lazy and did not learn Torah, it was as if הקדוש ברוך הוא became poor.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teacher, רבי אלעזר, brings his own opening verse for the מגילה. He reads it as a hint to the reason for the danger in the פורים story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the simple level, the verse is about a lazy homeowner whose roof falls in. רבי אלעזר reads 'rafters' as הקדוש ברוך הוא and 'sink' as 'become poor.' The point is that ישראל's laziness in Torah weakened, so to speak, the help that came to them from Above.

keyTerms.meaning: opened with an opening, meaning he introduced the topic with a verse
'the enemy of הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא', a respectful way of saying הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא Himself

steps.confusionAlert: 'The enemy of הקדוש ברוך הוא' does not mean a real enemy. It is a respectful way to avoid saying directly that הקדוש ברוך הוא became 'poor.'

Because of the laziness that Israel had,
that they did not occupy themselves with Torah,

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because ישראל neglected Torah study, the help they would have had from הקדוש ברוך הוא was weakened, and so the danger of the מגילה came.

steps.title: Proof that מך means poor and מקרה refers to God
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר brings two verses to back up his reading. In ויקרא, 'מך' means poor. In תהלים, 'המקרה' is used to describe הקדוש ברוך הוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'מך' always means poor, as the פסוק says: 'If he is too poor (מך) for the valuation.' 'מקרה' means הקדוש ברוך הוא, as the פסוק says: 'Who lays the beams (המקרה) of His chambers in the water.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows where רבי אלעזר got the two word meanings he used in the last step. It brings a separate verse for each word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reading depended on two unusual meanings. The first is that 'ימך' means 'become poor' and not 'sink.' The second is that 'המקרה', the rafters, refers to הקדוש ברוך הוא. Each meaning gets its own proof from another place in תנ״ך.

keyTerms.meaning: rafters or beams, here read as הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
'it is nothing but', a way of fixing a word's meaning
your valuation, from the laws of עֲרָכִין

phrases.english: And makh means nothing other than poor,
as it is stated: "But if he is too poor for the valuation,"
phrases.notes: This is from ויקרא, about a person who promised to give his value to the בית המקדש but is too poor to pay.

phrases.english: and mekare refers to none other than the Holy One, Blessed be He,
as it is stated: "Who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters."
phrases.notes: This is from תהלים, describing ה׳ building the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the two word meanings that רבי אלעזר's reading relied on.
steps.raayaObject: That 'מך' means poor and that 'המקרה' refers to הקדוש ברוך הוא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ויקרא 27:8 ('ואם מך הוא מערכך') and תהלים 104:3 ('המקרה במים עליותיו').

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק's opening: a man rose against us, not a king
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק opens with the verse in תהלים: 'Had ה׳ not been with us when a man rose against us.' He points out that it says 'a man' and not 'a king', which hints at המן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק opened this section with: 'A song of ascents. Had ה׳ not been with us, let Israel say. Had ה׳ not been with us when a man rose up against us.' It says 'a man' and not a king.
steps.whatsHappening: Another teacher gives his own opening verse for the מגילה. He builds it on one exact word, 'אדם', a man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse stresses that the enemy was 'a man', not a king. That fits המן, who was not the king but was the real enemy of ישראל. אחשורוש the king was not the main enemy.

keyTerms.meaning: a song of ascents, the title of some chapters in תְּהִלִּים
had it not been, or if not for
a man, and not a king, meaning הָמָן and not אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak opened with an opening
to this section from here:
"A song of ascents. If not for the Lord Who was with us,

If not for the Lord Who was with us

"A man" — and not a king.
phrases.notes: He means המן, the real enemy, who was not the king.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another, separate opening verse for the מגילה, following רבי אלעזר's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The verse's 'man who rose against us', not a king, hints at המן, the enemy saved from only by ה׳'s help.

steps.title: רבא's opening: joy with the righteous, sighing under the wicked
steps.stepSummary: רבא opens with the verse in משלי: 'When the righteous increase the people rejoice, and when the wicked rule the people sigh.' The righteous are מרדכי and אסתר, and the wicked one is המן. Each half is proven from a verse in the מגילה about the city of שושן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא opened this section with: 'When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when a wicked man rules, the people sigh.' The first half is מרדכי and אסתר, as it says, 'The city of שושן rejoiced and was glad.' The second half is המן, as it says, 'The city of שושן was confused.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another teacher, רבא, brings his opening verse. He matches each half of it to a different part of the מגילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reads the verse as a picture of the whole story. Under המן's rule, שושן was upset and confused. When מרדכי and אסתר rose to power, שושן celebrated. Each half has its own proof verse from the מגילה itself.

keyTerms.meaning: when the righteous increase or become great

steps.whatToRemember: All these openings point to one lesson. ישראל was weak in Torah and מצוות, the enemy was המן, and ה׳'s salvation through מרדכי and אסתר turned sadness into joy.

phrases.notes: This is from the מגילה, right after מרדכי came out dressed in royal clothes.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The verse's rejoicing over the righteous is מרדכי and אסתר, and the sighing under the wicked ruler is המן, each proven from the city of שושן's reaction in the מגילה.

steps.title: רב מתנה opens with a verse about God being close to His nation
steps.stepSummary: רב מתנה opens the מגילה with the verse ״כי מי גוי גדול אשר לו אלהים קרובים אליו״.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מתנה said: the opening comes from here: "For what nation is so great that has God so near to it."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more sage to the list of people who 'opened' the מגילה with an outside verse. רב מתנה picks a verse from ספר דברים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the openings in the earlier steps, this verse is meant as an introduction to the פורים story. The verse praises ישראל for having הקדוש ברוך הוא close to them. In the מגילה, He saved them even though His name is never mentioned.

keyTerms.meaning: From here (the source for his opening)

phrases.english: Rav Mattana said: from here:
phrases.notes: He means his opening verse for the מגילה comes from here, like the sages in the steps before.

phrases.english: "For what nation is so great
that has God so near to it."
phrases.notes: This פסוק is in ספר דברים, perek 4.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another opening verse to the series of פתיחתות that ended with רבא in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פורים story shows that ישראל has הקדוש ברוך הוא close to them, as the verse in דברים says.

steps.title: רב אשי opens with a verse about God taking a nation out of another nation
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי opens the מגילה with the verse ״או הנסה אלהים וגו׳״.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: the opening comes from here: "Or has God ventured, etc."
steps.whatsHappening: Another opening is added to the list. רב אשי brings another verse from the same perek in ספר דברים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The full verse continues 'to go and take for Himself a nation from the midst of another nation.' The ״וגו׳״ tells us to keep reading the verse. In the פורים story, הקדוש ברוך הוא saved ישראל while they lived among the Persians.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: from here:
"Or has God ventured, etc."
phrases.notes: The verse goes on: 'to take for Himself a nation from inside another nation.' That's the part that fits פורים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different opening verse right after רב מתנה's, from the same section of דברים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פורים rescue fits the verse about God taking a nation out from within another nation.
steps.whatToRemember: Each sage in this list picks an outside verse that sets up the פורים story. The list picks up again later with רבי לוי and רבי חייא (steps 17–18).

steps.title: רב reads 'ויהי' as a cry of woe
steps.stepSummary: On the first words ״ויהי בימי אחשורוש״, רב reads ״ויהי״ as ״וי והי״ (woe and grief) and connects it to the curse of being sold to enemies.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And it was in the days of אחשורוש." רב said: ויהי means 'woe and grief.' This is what is written: "And you will sell yourselves there to your enemies as slaves and maidservants, etc."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now starts explaining the מגילה itself, from its very first word. רב splits the word ״ויהי״ into two sounds of crying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״ויהי״ sounds like ״וי״ (woe) plus ״הי״ (grief), so the first word of the מגילה already warns that trouble is coming. רב ties this to the curse in ספר דברים where ישראל is sold to its enemies. In the מגילה, ישראל was 'sold' to המן.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was (first word of the מגילה)
And you will be sold / sell yourselves

phrases.english: "And it was in the days of Achashverosh"
phrases.notes: These are the very first words of the מגילה. Now the גמרא starts going through it.

phrases.english: Rav said: woe and grief,
phrases.notes: He's playing on the sound: ״ויהי״ heard as ״וי״ (woe) plus ״הי״ (a cry of grief).

phrases.english: this is what is written:
"And you will sell yourselves there to your enemies
phrases.notes: This is from the curses in ספר דברים, perek 28.

phrases.english: as slaves and maidservants, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ אָמַר רַב וַיי וְהֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the openings to explaining the first verse of the מגילה itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ״ויהי״ means ״וי והי״: the days of אחשורוש were a time of woe, fulfilling the curse of being sold to enemies.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the גמרא's style for the rest of the section: reading every word of the מגילה closely, even its first word.

steps.title: שמואל's hopeful verse matched to different exiles
steps.stepSummary: שמואל brings ״לא מאסתים ולא געלתים לכלותם״ and matches each phrase to a different time in Jewish history.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: "I will not reject them, nor will I hate them, to destroy them." "I will not reject them": in the days of the Greeks. "Nor will I hate them": in the days of נבוכדנצר. "To destroy them": in the days of המן. "To break My covenant with them": in the days of the Persians. "For I am ה׳ their God": in the days of גוג ומגוג.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gave a sad reading, and now שמואל gives a hopeful verse from ספר ויקרא instead. He splits the verse into parts and gives each part its own time period.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse promises that even in exile, הקדוש ברוך הוא won't throw ישראל away. שמואל shows the promise working again and again: under the Greeks, under נבוכדנצר, under המן, under the Persians, and finally at גוג ומגוג. For our מגילה, the key line is ״לכלותם״: in המן's time God did not let them be wiped out.

keyTerms.meaning: I hated / was disgusted by them
The great war at the end of days

steps.confusionAlert: The verse says 'I will NOT reject them.' Each time period is a time when ישראל could have been rejected, and God did not do it.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
"I will not reject them, nor will I hate them, to destroy them."
phrases.notes: This פסוק is in ויקרא, perek 26, right after the long list of curses.

phrases.english: "I will not reject them": in the days of the Greeks.
"Nor will I hate them": in the days of Nebuchadnezzar.
"To destroy them": in the days of Haman.
"To break My covenant with them": in the days of the Persians.
phrases.notes: This phrase comes later in the same verse. The verse continues past the part quoted above.

phrases.aramaic: ״כִּי אֲנִי ה׳ אֱלֹהֵיהֶם״ — בִּימֵי גוֹג וּמָגוֹג.
phrases.english: "For I am ה׳ their God": in the days of Gog and Magog.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר לֹא מְאַסְתִּים וְלֹא גְעַלְתִּים לְכַלּוֹתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: שמואל gives his own verse alongside רב's ״וי והי״, with a hopeful message instead of a sad one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each phrase of ״לא מאסתים...״ refers to a different exile in which God did not abandon ישראל; ״לכלותם״ is the time of המן.

steps.title: A ברייתא matches the same verse to exiles and the leaders God sent
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא matches the parts of ״לא מאסתים...״ to different periods, and names the leaders הקדוש ברוך הוא gave ישראל in each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: "I will not reject them": in the days of the Chaldeans, when I gave them דניאל, חנניה, מישאל and עזריה. "Nor will I hate them": in the days of the Greeks, when I gave them שמעון הצדיק, the Chashmonai and his sons, and מתתיה the כהן גדול. "To destroy them": in the days of המן, when I gave them מרדכי and אסתר. "To break My covenant with them": in the days of the Romans, when I gave them the sages of the house of רבי and the sages of each generation. "For I am ה׳ their God": in the future, when no nation or people will be able to rule over them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that reads the same verse as שמואל but matches the parts to somewhat different periods. It also adds who God sent to help in each period.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא explains how God 'did not reject' ישראל: in every exile He gave them righteous leaders. Both שמואל and the ברייתא connect ״לכלותם״ to המן, and here the saviors are named, מרדכי and אסתר. The last phrase is moved to the future, when no nation will rule over ישראל at all.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the משנה)
When I set up for them (leaders)

steps.whatToRemember: רב sees ״ויהי״ as a cry of woe, while שמואל and the ברייתא stress God's promise never to abandon ישראל. In the days of המן, God kept that promise through מרדכי and אסתר.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita:
"I will not reject them": in the days of the Chaldeans,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֶעֱמַדְתִּי לָהֶם דָּנִיֵּאל חֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה.
phrases.english: when I set up for them Daniel, Chananya, Mishael and Azarya.
"Nor will I hate them": in the days of the Greeks,
when I set up for them Shimon HaTzaddik,
and the Chashmonai and his sons, and Mattityahu the Kohen Gadol.
"To destroy them": in the days of Haman,
when I set up for them Mordechai and Esther.
"To break My covenant with them": in the days of the Romans,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֶעֱמַדְתִּי לָהֶם שֶׁל בֵּית רַבִּי וְחַכְמֵי דוֹרוֹת.
phrases.english: when I set up for them those of the house of Rabbi and the sages of the generations.
phrases.notes: 'רבי' here means רבי יהודה הנשיא and his family of leaders.

phrases.english: "For I am ה׳ their God": in the future to come,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין כׇּל אוּמָּה וְלָשׁוֹן יְכוֹלָה לִשְׁלוֹט בָּהֶם.
phrases.english: when no nation or people will be able to rule over them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of שמואל's reading of the same verse, changing some of the periods and naming the leaders God sent in each.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In each exile God showed He had not rejected ישראל by giving them righteous leaders; in המן's time these were מרדכי and אסתר, and in the future no nation will rule over ישראל.

steps.title: רבי לוי's opening verse: driving out the people of the land
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי opens the מגילה with the verse warning what happens if the Jews do not drive out the inhabitants of the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי לוי said his opening comes from here: 'But if you will not drive out the inhabitants of the land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues its list of opening verses for the מגילה. Now רבי לוי gives his choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רב מתנה and רב אשי before him, רבי לוי picks a verse to introduce the story of פורים. His verse warns that enemies who are left alive will cause trouble later. It hints that the danger in the מגילה came from an enemy that was never fully removed.

keyTerms.meaning: From here (this is the verse he uses to open)
The people living in the land

phrases.english: Rabbi Levi said: from here:
phrases.notes: 'From here' means this is the verse he uses to open the מגילה, like the rabbis in the steps before.

phrases.english: “But if you will not drive out the inhabitants of the land.”
phrases.notes: This is from במדבר 33:55. The verse goes on to say that the ones left behind will be like thorns in your eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another rabbi's opening verse to the list of openings for the מגילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מגילה can be introduced with במדבר 33:55, the warning about not driving out the inhabitants of the land.

steps.title: רבי חייא's opening verse: what I planned for them I will do to you
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא opens with the very next verse: what God planned to do to the nations, He will do to the Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא said his opening comes from here: 'And it shall be that as I thought to do to them, I will do to you.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another rabbi gives his opening verse for the מגילה. רבי חייא picks the verse that comes right after רבי לוי's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי לוי's verse warned that enemies left behind would cause trouble. רבי חייא's verse goes one step further: the punishment meant for the enemies can turn onto the Jews themselves. This fits the threat in the מגילה, when the Jews were in danger of being destroyed.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya said: from here:
“And it shall be, as I thought
to do to them, so I will do to you.”
phrases.notes: This is במדבר 33:56, the very next verse after the one רבי לוי quoted. 'Them' means the nations of the land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another opening verse, taken from the verse right after רבי לוי's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מגילה can be introduced with במדבר 33:56: what God planned for the nations He will do to Israel.

steps.title: רב: אחשורוש is the brother and match of נבוכדנצר
steps.stepSummary: רב reads the name אחשורוש as 'brother of the head' and 'the same kind as the head.' The 'head' is נבוכדנצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'אחשורוש': רב said: the brother of the 'head,' and the match of the 'head.' The brother of the head means the brother of the wicked נבוכדנצר, who is called 'head,' as it says, 'You are the head of gold.' The match of the head: נבוכדנצר killed Jews, and אחשורוש wanted to kill them. נבוכדנצר destroyed, and אחשורוש wanted to destroy, as it says, 'And in the reign of אחשורוש, at the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the people of יהודה and ירושלים.'
steps.whatsHappening: The openings are done. The גמרא continues explaining the מגילה word by word and now reaches the king's name, אחשורוש. רב explains it first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב hears 'אח' (brother) and 'ראש' (head) inside the name. The 'head' is נבוכדנצר, because דניאל called him 'the head of gold.' So אחשורוש is like a brother to him: נבוכדנצר killed Jews and destroyed, and אחשורוש wanted to do the same things. The verse from עזרא shows that in אחשורוש's time there was a push against the Jews in יהודה and ירושלים.

keyTerms.meaning: Head; here a name for נבוכדנצר
His match; someone just like him (literally 'son of his age')
The head of gold (Aramaic, from דניאל)

steps.confusionAlert: The word 'הוא' (he) appears twice in each pair. The first 'he' is נבוכדנצר, who actually did it. The second 'he' is אחשורוש, who only wanted to.

phrases.english: “Achashverosh”: Rav said:
the brother of the 'head,'
phrases.notes: רב splits the name into pieces: אח (brother) and ראש (head).

phrases.english: and the match of the 'head.'
'The brother of the head' means:
the brother of the wicked Nebuchadnezzar,
who is called 'head,' as it says:
“You are the head of gold.”
phrases.notes: This is from דניאל 2:38, where דניאל tells נבוכדנצר that he is the golden head of the statue in his dream.

phrases.english: 'The match of the head' means:
he killed, and he wanted to kill;
phrases.notes: The first 'he' is נבוכדנצר and the second 'he' is אחשורוש.

phrases.english: he destroyed, and he wanted to destroy,
as it says: “And in the reign of Achashverosh,
at the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation
against the people living in Judah and Jerusalem.”
phrases.notes: This is from עזרא 4:6, where enemies wrote to the king to stop the Jews from rebuilding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the opening verses to explaining the words of the מגילה, starting with the king's name. Step 14 already explained the word before it, ויהי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name אחשורוש means 'brother of the head': he was the brother and match of נבוכדנצר, wanting to kill and destroy just as נבוכדנצר did.

steps.title: שמואל: Israel's faces were blackened in his days
steps.stepSummary: שמואל hears the word 'black' in the name אחשורוש: the Jews' faces turned black like the bottom of a pot.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: the name means that the faces of ישראל were blackened in his days, like the bottom of a pot.
steps.whatsHappening: A second explanation of the name אחשורוש. שמואל reads a different word inside it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of 'brother of the head,' שמואל hears שחור (black) in the name. Blackened faces describe the fear and shame of the Jews during his rule. It is as dark as the sooty bottom of a cooking pot.

keyTerms.meaning: The bottom of a pot (black from the fire)

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
that the faces of Israel were blackened
phrases.notes: שמואל hears the word שחור, 'black,' hiding inside the name אחשורוש.

phrases.english: in his days, like the bottom of a pot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different explanation of the same name that רב explained.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name אחשורוש hints that Israel's faces were blackened in his days.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: whoever remembers him says 'woe to his head'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reads the name as 'אח לראשו,' a cry of 'woe to his head' said by anyone who remembers him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: everyone who remembers him says, 'Woe to his head!'
steps.whatsHappening: A third explanation of the name אחשורוש. רבי יוחנן reads it as a curse people say about him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן also hears אח and ראש, like רב did. But for him 'אח' is not 'brother.' It is a cry of pain, so the name becomes 'woe to his head,' meaning people remember him badly.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Whoever remembers him says, “Woe to his head!”
phrases.notes: Here 'אח' is a cry like 'ah!' or 'woe!', not 'brother' as in רב's reading.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third reading of the name. It uses the same letters as רב's reading but gives אח a different meaning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name אחשורוש means 'woe to his head,' since everyone who remembers him curses him.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: everyone became poor in his days
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא hears 'רש' (poor) in the name and proves from the verse that אחשורוש put a tax on everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי חנינא said: the name means that everyone became poor in his days, as it says, 'And King אחשורוש laid a tax.'
steps.whatsHappening: A fourth and last explanation of the name אחשורוש. רבי חנינא backs it up with a verse from the end of the מגילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא hears רש (a poor person) in the name. His proof is the verse that says אחשורוש placed a tax on the land, which made people poor. So the name itself tells us what life was like under him.
steps.whatToRemember: All four explanations of the name אחשורוש (רב, שמואל, רבי יוחנן, רבי חנינא) find a hidden word in it, and each one shows that his reign was bad for the Jews.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Chanina said:
that everyone became poor in his days,
phrases.notes: רש means a poor person. רבי חנינא hears it at the end of the name אחשורוש.

phrases.english: as it says: “And King Achashverosh laid a tax.”
phrases.notes: This is from אסתר 10:1, near the very end of the מגילה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The last of four readings of the name. This one is supported by a verse from the מגילה itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name אחשורוש hints that everyone became poor in his days, because he placed a tax on the land.

steps.title: The word 'This is' shows the wicked stayed wicked
steps.stepSummary: The word 'הוא' in 'הוא אחשורוש' teaches that he stayed wicked from beginning to end. The same word does the same thing for עשו, דתן ואבירם, and המלך אחז.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'This is אחשורוש': he stayed in his wickedness from beginning to end. 'This is עשו': he stayed in his wickedness from beginning to end. 'This is דתן ואבירם': they stayed in their wickedness from beginning to end. 'This is the king אחז': he stayed in his wickedness from beginning to end.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the extra word 'הוא' in the first פסוק of the מגילה and shows that the same word works the same way in other פסוקים about wicked people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have just said 'אחשורוש'; the added 'הוא' ('this is the same one') is read as saying he never changed. The גמרא backs this up with three more פסוקים where 'הוא' describes wicked people, so it is a pattern, not a one-time reading.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is' or 'he is the same one': a sign that the person stayed the same
From his beginning to his end, his whole life
The two troublemakers who fought משה in the מדבר and joined קרח

phrases.english: "This is Achashverosh"
phrases.notes: This is the opening פסוק of the מגילה (אסתר א:א), the same verse the גמרא has been working on.

phrases.english: he remained in his wickedness
from his beginning until his end.
"This is Esav"
phrases.notes: From the list of עשו's family in בראשית (לו:מג).

phrases.english: he remained in his wickedness from his beginning until his end.
"This is Dasan and Aviram"
phrases.notes: From במדבר (כו:ט), where they are mentioned along with קרח.

phrases.english: they remained in their wickedness from their beginning until their end.
"This is the king Achaz"
phrases.notes: From דברי הימים ב (כח:כב). אחז was a wicked king of יהודה.

phrases.english: he remained in his wickedness from his beginning until his end.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ — הוּא בְּרִשְׁעוֹ מִתְּחִילָּתוֹ וְעַד סוֹפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After reading the name אחשורוש itself in steps 19 to 22, the גמרא now reads the word 'הוא' that comes before it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'הוא' before a wicked person's name means he stayed wicked his whole life.

steps.title: The same word shows the righteous stayed righteous
steps.stepSummary: The word 'הוא' also works for good people: אברהם, and אהרן ומשה, stayed righteous from beginning to end.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'אברם, this is אברהם': he stayed in his righteousness from beginning to end. 'This is אהרן and משה': they stayed in their righteousness from beginning to end.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that 'הוא' is not only a negative sign. It also describes righteous people who never changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is now clearly about not changing, whether good or bad. Even though אברם's name was changed to אברהם, the פסוק's 'הוא' tells us he was the same צדיק before and after.

keyTerms.meaning: 'אברם, this is אברהם': the same person under his old and new names

phrases.english: "Avram, this is Avraham"
phrases.notes: From דברי הימים א (א:כז). The name changed, but the person stayed the same.

phrases.english: he remained in his righteousness from his beginning until his end.
"This is Aharon and Moshe"
phrases.notes: From שמות (ו:כו).

phrases.english: they remained in their righteousness from their beginning until their end.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבְרָם הוּא אַבְרָהָם — הוּא בְּצִדְקוֹ מִתְּחִילָּתוֹ וְעַד סוֹפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips the pattern from step 23 to the righteous side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'הוא' before a righteous person's name means he stayed righteous his whole life.

steps.title: דוד stayed humble even as king
steps.stepSummary: 'ודוד הוא הקטן' teaches that דוד stayed humble his whole life. As a young man he bowed to anyone greater in תורה, and as king he bowed to anyone greater in wisdom.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And דוד, he was the small one': he stayed in his smallness from beginning to end. Just as when he was young he made himself small before anyone greater than him in תורה, so too as king he made himself small before anyone greater than him in wisdom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the 'הוא' rule to דוד, and it explains what 'small' really means here: humility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply, 'הקטן' means 'the youngest' of ישי's sons. The גמרא reads 'הוא' as saying he stayed 'small' all his life, meaning humble. Becoming king did not change how he treated people who knew more than him.

keyTerms.meaning: The small one: here, the youngest, read as the humble one
His smallness: his youth, and also his humility
He made himself small, he humbled himself
His kingship, the time he was king

steps.whatToRemember: The word 'הוא' before a name means the person never changed. The wicked stayed wicked (אחשורוש, עשו, דתן ואבירם, אחז), the righteous stayed righteous (אברהם, אהרן ומשה), and דוד stayed humble even as king.
steps.confusionAlert: 'קטנותו' is used in two senses here. In 'כשם שבקטנותו' it means 'when he was young,' but in 'הוא בקטנותו' it means 'his humility.' Both are playing on the same word.

phrases.english: "And David, he was the small one"
phrases.notes: From שמואל א (יז:יד). Simply, it says דוד was the youngest of ישי's sons.

phrases.english: he remained in his smallness from his beginning until his end,
phrases.notes: Here 'smallness' means humility. He never acted big.

phrases.english: just as in his youth he made himself small
before anyone who was greater than him in Torah,
so too in his kingship he made himself small
before anyone who was greater than him in wisdom.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדָוִד הוּא הַקָּטָן — הוּא בְּקַטְנוּתוֹ מִתְּחִילָּתוֹ עַד סוֹפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The last example of the 'הוא' pattern, adding a lesson about humility.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד stayed humble his whole life, even as king, before anyone greater than him.

steps.title: רב: 'Who reigned' means he made himself king
steps.stepSummary: רב reads 'המולך' as 'he became king on his own,' without inheriting the throne. Some take this as praise, others as criticism.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Who reigned': רב said, he became king by himself. Some say this as praise, and some say it as criticism.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next word of the פסוק, 'המולך,' and gives רב's reading. It then says there are two ways to take it, which the next step will explain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'המולך' sounds like 'the one who made himself king,' meaning he did not get the crown from his father. Step 27 explains why that could be a good thing or a bad thing.

keyTerms.meaning: He became king on his own, not by inheriting

phrases.english: "Who reigned"
phrases.notes: The next word in the same opening פסוק: 'הוא אחשורוש המולך מהודו ועד כוש.'

phrases.english: Rav said: That he became king on his own.
Some say it as praise
and some say it as criticism.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the word 'הוא' to the next word in the פסוק, 'המולך.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'המולך' means אחשורוש became king on his own; this can be read as praise or as criticism.

steps.title: Why it could be praise and why it could be criticism
steps.stepSummary: Praise: there was nobody else as fit to be king as he was. Criticism: he was not fit to be king, but he paid a lot of money and got the throne that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Those who say it as praise: there was no man as fit to be king as he was. Those who say it as criticism: he was not fit to rule, but he paid a lot of extra money and rose to power.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains the two sides it mentioned in the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree he was not born into the crown. The question is how he got it: by being the best man for the job, or by buying it with money.

keyTerms.meaning: And he rose up (to the throne)

phrases.english: Those who say it as praise:

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא הֲוָה אִינִישׁ דַּחֲשִׁיב לְמַלְכָּא כְּווֹתֵיהּ,
phrases.english: that there was no man as worthy to be king as he was,
and those who say it as criticism:
that he was not fit for kingship,
but he gave a lot of extra money and rose up.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי לַהּ לְשֶׁבַח — דְּלָא הֲוָה אִינִישׁ דַּחֲשִׁיב לְמַלְכָּא כְּווֹתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the 'praise' and 'criticism' readings that step 26 only mentioned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Praise: he was the most fit to rule. Criticism: he was unfit and bought the throne.

steps.title: First view: הודו and כוש are at opposite ends of the world
steps.stepSummary: On 'מהודו ועד כוש,' רב and שמואל disagree. One says הודו is at one end of the world and כוש is at the other end.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'From הודו to כוש': רב and שמואל disagree. One said: הודו is at the end of the world and כוש is at the end of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reaches the next words of the פסוק and brings a disagreement between רב and שמואל. This step gives the first opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this view, the פסוק is simply measuring his kingdom: it stretched from one far edge of the world to the other. We are not told which of the two אמוראים said which view.

keyTerms.meaning: The end of the world, its far edge

phrases.english: "From Hodu to Kush"
phrases.notes: The last words of the same opening פסוק, describing where אחשורוש ruled.

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel disagree:
one said:
Hodu is at the end of the world
and Kush is at the end of the world,

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵהוֹדּוּ וְעַד כּוּשׁ, רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next phrase of the פסוק and opens a disagreement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One view: הודו and כוש are at opposite ends of the world, so the פסוק shows the full size of his kingdom.

steps.title: Second view: הודו and כוש are next to each other
steps.stepSummary: The other opinion says הודו and כוש are neighbors. The פסוק means that just as he ruled those two lands easily, he ruled the whole world just as easily.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one said: הודו and כוש are right next to each other. Just as he ruled over הודו and כוש, so too he ruled from one end of the world to the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second side of the disagreement between רב and שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the two lands are neighbors, the פסוק is not measuring distance. Instead it is a comparison: ruling the whole world was as easy for him as ruling two countries side by side. Both views agree he ruled the whole world; they differ on what the words 'מהודו ועד כוש' are telling us.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as ... so too: a comparison

steps.whatToRemember: 'המולך' means אחשורוש made himself king (praise: he was the most worthy; criticism: he bought the throne). On 'מהודו ועד כוש,' one view says these lands are at opposite ends of the world, and the other says they are neighbors, so he ruled the whole world as easily as two neighboring lands.
steps.confusionAlert: The second view does not say his kingdom was small. It agrees he ruled the whole world, and uses the two neighboring lands only as a picture of how easily he did it.

phrases.english: And one said:

phrases.aramaic: הוֹדּוּ וְכוּשׁ גַּבֵּי הֲדָדֵי הֲווֹ קָיְימִי;
phrases.english: Hodu and Kush stand next to each other;
just as he ruled over Hodu and Kush,

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ מָלַךְ מִסּוֹף הָעוֹלָם וְעַד סוֹפוֹ.
phrases.english: so too he ruled from one end of the world to its other end.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחַד אָמַר: הוֹדּוּ וְכוּשׁ גַּבֵּי הֲדָדֵי הֲווֹ קָיְימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the רב and שמואל disagreement from step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Second view: הודו and כוש are neighbors; just as he ruled them easily, he ruled the whole world easily.

steps.title: The same argument about שלמה's kingdom: one end of the world to the other
steps.stepSummary: The same disagreement shows up on the פסוק about שלמה ruling 'from תפסח to עזה.' One opinion says these places are at opposite ends of the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the same way you can read: 'For he ruled over all the land across the river, from תפסח to עזה.' רב and שמואל disagree. One says תפסח is at one end of the world and עזה is at the other end.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second פסוק, about שלמה, that רב and שמואל argue about in exactly the same way as 'הודו to כוש.' Here we hear the first opinion: the two places are at opposite ends of the world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a parallel to Steps 28-29. The question is the same: do the two places in the פסוק mark the outer edges of the kingdom? This opinion says yes, so the פסוק itself is telling us the kingdom covered the whole world.

keyTerms.meaning: Tiphsah, a place named in the פסוק about שלמה

phrases.english: Similarly, you say:
"For he ruled over all the land across the river
phrases.notes: This פסוק is about שלמה המלך, in מלכים א.

phrases.english: from Tiphsah until Gaza"
Rav and Shmuel disagree:
phrases.notes: The word 'disagree' isn't written, but the גמרא means it, just like in the הודו and כוש argument.

phrases.english: One said: Tiphsah is at one end of the world
and Gaza is at the other end of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel פסוק on which רב and שמואל argue the same way as about הודו and כוש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to one opinion, תפסח and עזה are at opposite ends of the world, so שלמה ruled the whole world.

steps.title: The other opinion: תפסח and עזה are neighbors
steps.stepSummary: The second opinion says תפסח and עזה are right next to each other. Just as שלמה ruled those two places easily, he ruled the whole world just as easily.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other one says: תפסח and עזה are right next to each other. Just as he ruled over תפסח and עזה, so he ruled over the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second side of the argument. It says the two places are close together, so the פסוק is making a comparison, not drawing a map.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the two places are neighbors, naming them can't show how big the kingdom was. So this opinion reads the פסוק as a comparison: his rule over the whole world was as smooth and easy as ruling two nearby towns.
steps.whatToRemember: The argument about שלמה ('from תפסח to עזה') matches the argument about אחשורוש ('from הודו to כוש'): either the places are far apart and show the size of the kingdom, or they are neighbors and show how easily he ruled.

phrases.english: And the other one said:

phrases.aramaic: תִּפְסַח וְעַזָּה בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי הֲווֹ קָיְימִי;
phrases.english: Tiphsah and Gaza are located right next to each other;

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁמָּלַךְ עַל תִּפְסַח וְעַל עַזָּה,
phrases.english: just as he ruled over Tiphsah and over Gaza,

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ מָלַךְ עַל כׇּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ.
phrases.english: so too he ruled over the entire world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion to Step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תפסח and עזה are neighbors. The פסוק means שלמה ruled the whole world as easily as he ruled these two places.

steps.title: רב חסדא: the 127 provinces came in three stages
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא reads 'seven and twenty and a hundred provinces' as three stages. אחשורוש first ruled 7 provinces, then 20 more, then 100 more.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Seven and twenty and a hundred provinces.' רב חסדא said: At first he ruled over seven, then over twenty more, and finally over a hundred more.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the opening פסוק of the מגילה and explains its unusual way of counting the provinces.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have just said '127.' רב חסדא reads each number as its own stage, so the kingdom grew step by step over time.

phrases.english: "Seven and twenty and a hundred provinces"
phrases.notes: This is the end of the first פסוק of the מגילה, about אחשורוש.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
At first he ruled over seven provinces,
and then he ruled over twenty more,
and finally he ruled over a hundred more.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the next phrase of the opening פסוק of the מגילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The number 127 is split up to show that אחשורוש's kingdom grew in three stages: 7, then 20, then 100.

steps.title: Challenge from עמרם's age, written the same way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: עמרם's age is also written as 'seven and thirty and a hundred years.' Would you split that up into stages too?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, what about 'And the years of עמרם's life were seven and thirty and a hundred years'? What would you learn from that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא. The same counting style appears in the תורה for עמרם's age, and nobody learns anything special from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the style of 'seven and twenty and a hundred' is enough for a דרשה, then עמרם's age should get one too. But that is just the normal way the תורה writes numbers, so maybe the פסוק in אסתר is normal as well.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (a challenge: if your logic is right, then...)
What would you learn out of it?

phrases.english: But if that is so,
"And the years of the life of Amram
phrases.notes: This פסוק is in פרשת וארא, in שמות.

phrases.english: were seven and thirty and a hundred years"
what would you learn from it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב חסדא's reading in Step 32.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's drawing a lesson from the 'seven and twenty and a hundred' wording
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same wording is used for עמרם's age with no lesson, so the wording alone can't be a basis for a דרשה.

steps.title: Answer: in the מגילה the number is extra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the פסוק in אסתר is different. 'From הודו to כוש' already tells us how big the kingdom was, so the number of provinces is extra and is there to teach something.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different here, because the words are extra. Since it already says 'from הודו to כוש,' why do I need 'seven and twenty and a hundred provinces'? Learn from this that it comes for a דרשה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב חסדא. The lesson does not come from the counting style. It comes from the fact that the number is not needed in the פסוק at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With עמרם, the number is the only way we learn his age, so it is needed and teaches nothing extra. In the מגילה, 'from הודו to כוש' already describes the kingdom, so the extra number is free to teach that the kingdom grew in stages.

keyTerms.meaning: A lesson learned from the words of a פסוק

steps.confusionAlert: The דרשה is NOT based on the strange order 'seven and twenty and a hundred.' That style is normal, as עמרם's age shows. It works only because the whole phrase is extra in this פסוק.
steps.whatToRemember: An unusual style alone is not enough for a דרשה. But when words in a פסוק are extra, they can be used to teach a lesson.

phrases.english: It is different here, because this part of the verse is extra:
since it already says "from Hodu to Cush,"
why do I need "seven and twenty and a hundred provinces"?
Learn from this that it is there for a lesson.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from עמרם in Step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the words in the מגילה are extra, while עמרם's age is needed information.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'seven and twenty and a hundred' style alone was the basis of the lesson, so עמרם's age should teach something too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lesson comes from the extra wording in the מגילה. 'From הודו to כוש' already describes the kingdom, so the number is free to teach the three stages.

steps.title: ברייתא: three kings ruled the whole world
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that three kings ruled over the whole world: אחאב, אחשורוש and נבוכדנצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Three kings ruled over the whole world, and these are they: אחאב, אחשורוש and נבוכדנצר.
steps.whatsHappening: Since we have been talking about kings ruling the whole world, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists three such kings. This sets up the next steps, which give a source for each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא makes a claim, and the following lines back it up with a פסוק for each king. אחשורוש is on the list because of what we already learned about his kingdom.

keyTerms.meaning: Ruled over the whole world, literally 'under the dome' of the sky

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Three kings ruled over the whole world,
phrases.notes: Literally 'under the dome,' meaning everything under the sky.

phrases.english: and they are: Ahab, Ahasuerus, and Nebuchadnezzar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related topic: kings who ruled the entire world.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three kings ruled the whole world: אחאב, אחשורוש and נבוכדנצר.

steps.title: Proof that אחאב ruled the world: he made every nation swear
steps.stepSummary: עובדיה told אליהו that אחאב searched for him in every nation and kingdom and made them swear. A king can only make people swear if he rules over them.
steps.simpleTranslation: אחאב, as it is written: 'As ה׳ your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my master did not send to look for you...' If he did not rule over them, how could he make them swear?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a proof from a פסוק that אחאב ruled the whole world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rest of the פסוק says אחאב made each nation swear they had not found אליהו. The גמרא reasons that you can't force a nation to swear unless you rule over it. So אחאב must have ruled every nation.

phrases.english: Ahab, as it is written:
"As the Lord your God lives,
phrases.notes: עובדיה, אחאב's servant, is speaking to אליהו הנביא.

phrases.english: there is no nation or kingdom

phrases.aramaic: אֲשֶׁר לֹא שָׁלַח אֲדוֹנִי שָׁם לְבַקֶּשְׁךָ וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: where my master has not sent to look for you, etc."
phrases.notes: The part the גמרא needs comes later in the פסוק: 'he made the kingdom and nation swear that they had not found you.'

phrases.english: And if he did not rule over them,
how could he have made them swear?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the first king in the ברייתא's list.
steps.raayaObject: That אחאב ruled the whole world
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א יח:י, where אחאב makes every nation and kingdom swear they had not found אליהו

steps.title: Proof for נבוכדנצר, and אחשורוש from what we already learned
steps.stepSummary: ירמיהו says any nation that will not put its neck under the yoke of the king of בבל will be punished, which shows נבוכדנצר ruled everyone. For אחשורוש, the proof is what we already said.
steps.simpleTranslation: נבוכדנצר, as it is written: 'And the nation and the kingdom that will not put its neck under the yoke of the king of בבל...' אחשורוש, as we said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes backing up the ברייתא. It gives a פסוק for נבוכדנצר and points back to earlier steps for אחשורוש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ירמיהו speaks of every nation needing to submit to בבל, so נבוכדנצר's rule reached the whole world. For אחשורוש, the גמרא points back to the 'from הודו to כוש' discussion, where both views agreed he ruled from one end of the world to the other.

keyTerms.meaning: A yoke, meaning being under someone's control

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's three world rulers are each proven: אחאב by making every nation swear, נבוכדנצר by the yoke of בבל in ירמיהו, and אחשורוש by the 'הודו to כוש' discussion above.

phrases.english: Nebuchadnezzar, as it is written:
"And it shall be that the nation and the kingdom
phrases.notes: This is from ירמיהו, warning every nation to submit to בבל.

phrases.english: that will not put its neck
under the yoke of the king of Babylonia."
Ahasuerus, as we said.
phrases.notes: He means the earlier discussion of 'from הודו to כוש,' which showed אחשורוש ruled the whole world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the sources for the ברייתא, covering the remaining two kings.
steps.raayaObject: That נבוכדנצר and אחשורוש ruled the whole world
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו כז:ח for נבוכדנצר, and the earlier 'מהודו ועד כוש' discussion for אחשורוש
